segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Festus, three days after arriving in the province, went up from Caesarea to Jerusalem,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and the chief priests and the leading men of the Jews laid charges against Paul before him. They kept urging him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: asking as a favor against Paul that he send for him to come to Jerusalem—they were planning an ambush to kill him on the way.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Festus replied that Paul was being held at Caesarea and that he himself intended to leave for there soon.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “So let the men of standing among you come down with me,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: he said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “and if there is anything improper about the man, let them accuse him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After spending no more than eight or ten days among them, he went down to Caesarea, and the next day he took his seat on the tribunal and ordered Paul to be brought in.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Paul arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many serious charges that they were unable to prove,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: while Paul said in his defense,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I have committed no offense against the law of the Jews, or against the temple, or against Caesar.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Festus, wanting to do the Jews a favor, answered Paul,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem and be tried there on these charges before me?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I am standing before Caesar’s tribunal, where I ought to be tried. I have done the Jews no wrong, as you yourself know very well.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: If, then, I am in the wrong and have done something deserving death, I do not refuse to die. But if there is nothing in what these men accuse me of, no one can hand me over to them as a favor. I appeal to Caesar.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Festus, after conferring with his council, answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You have appealed to Caesar; to Caesar you will go.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After some days had passed, King Agrippa and Bernice arrived at Caesarea to pay their respects to Festus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Since they were staying there for several days, Festus laid Paul’s case before the king, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “There is a man here whom Felix left behind as a prisoner.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: When I was in Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews laid charges against him, asking for a sentence of condemnation against him.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I answered them that it is not the custom of Romans to hand over any person as a favor before the accused has faced his accusers in person and has had the opportunity to defend himself against the charge.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So when they assembled here, I allowed no delay: the next day I took my seat on the tribunal and ordered the man to be brought in.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: When the accusers stood up, they brought no charge against him of the kind of crimes I had suspected;

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: instead they had some disputes with him about their own religion and about a certain Jesus, who had died but whom Paul claimed was alive.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Since I was at a loss how to investigate these matters, I asked whether he would be willing to go to Jerusalem and be tried there on these charges.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But when Paul appealed to be held for the Emperor’s decision, I ordered him to be held until I could send him up to Caesar.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Agrippa said to Festus,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I would like to hear the man myself.”

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Tomorrow,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: he said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “you will hear him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pageantry and entered the audience hall along with the military tribunes and the most prominent men of the city. Then Festus gave the order, and Paul was brought in.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Festus said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “King Agrippa and all you who are present with us, you see this man, about whom the whole community of the Jews petitioned me, both in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he ought not to live any longer.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But I found that he had done nothing deserving death, and when he himself appealed to the Emperor, I decided to send him.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But I have nothing definite to write to my lord about him. So I have brought him before you all, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that after the examination has been held I may have something to write.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For it seems to me unreasonable to send a prisoner without also indicating the charges against him.”

notes.note: The word names the raised platform from which a Roman magistrate heard cases; a ruling given from it was official. “Judgment seat” is the older English rendering, and several modern versions already use “tribunal.” Taking his seat there marks the hearing as a formal trial.

notes.phrase: hand me over to them as a favor
notes.note: Most versions say “give me up” or “hand me over.” The Greek verb means to grant something as a favor, and it echoes the noun “favor” in verses 3 and 9: Paul is saying that he is not a gift the governor may make to his accusers. The same verb is used in verse 16.

A Roman citizen facing a capital charge in the provinces could ask to have his case transferred to the emperor’s court in Rome. Once the appeal was accepted, the governor could no longer dispose of the case himself. “Caesar” is the emperor’s title; the emperor at this time was Nero.

This is Herod Agrippa II, son of the Herod whose death is told in Acts 12 and great-grandson of Herod the Great. Bernice was his sister. He ruled territories to the north and east under Roman patronage and had the right to appoint the Jewish high priest, which is why Festus treats him as an expert on Jewish matters.

notes.phrase: the kind of crimes I had suspected
notes.note: The manuscripts differ over the word rendered “crimes” here: it appears in more than one grammatical form, and some manuscripts lack it altogether. The sense is little affected either way—the accusers brought none of the charges Festus had expected.

The Greek word can be neutral (“religion,” “reverence for the divine”) or dismissive (“superstition”), and older versions chose the latter. Since Festus is speaking courteously to a Jewish king, the neutral sense is more likely, and most modern translations agree. “Their own” could also be read as “his own,” meaning Paul’s.

The Greek word is the equivalent of the Latin title “Augustus,” borne by every Roman emperor after the first. Older versions print “Augustus,” which a modern reader is likely to take as the name of the first emperor, who was long dead. The reigning emperor was Nero. The word differs from “Caesar” at the end of the verse, so the two are rendered differently.

Festus refers to the emperor simply as “the lord.” This way of referring to the emperor was becoming common in the eastern provinces at about this time. It is lowercase here because it does not refer to God or to Jesus, though early Christian readers would have noticed the same title they gave to Jesus.

candidates.reason: Recurs in the Gospels, Acts, Romans 14:10 and 2 Corinthians 5:10, where versions vary between “judgment seat,” “tribunal,” “court” and “bench.”
Used for Roman cohort commanders throughout Acts 21–25 and more loosely in Mark, John and Revelation; versions vary between “tribune,” “commander” and “captain.”
Translators split between “Caesar” and “the emperor” across the Gospels, Acts and Philippians, and readers should see one consistent choice.
The plural (“chief priests”) and singular (“high priest”) are conventionally rendered with different English words, and this needs a single rule across the Gospels, Acts and Hebrews.
Covers Jewish council elders, church officers and simply older people; a single policy is needed on “elder” versus “presbyter” or “older man.”
